659.title: Agni, the witness
659.hook: Sita answers Rama, and calls the fire to witness her heart
659.howItsDone: At a Hindu wedding the couple walk around a sacred fire and make their vows with Agni as witness. The agni-parīkṣā, Sita's trial by fire, is retold and debated in homes, temples, classrooms and women's songs; different Ramayanas tell it differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fire began with words: raja dharma, and the freedom to question it. Rama spoke coldly to Sita in front of everyone, and she wept. Today, her answer.
screen: `RAJA DHARMA, AND THE FREEDOM TO QUESTION IT.`

segments.voice: Sita wipes her tears. The crowd is silent: monkeys, bears, rakshasas, Lakshmana, Sugriva, Vibhishana, all waiting. And when she speaks, in Valmiki, her voice is steady. She doesn't beg. She doesn't apologize. She asks her husband a question: why are you talking to me the way a common man talks to a common woman? Then, point by point, in front of the same crowd that heard him, she answers everything he said.
screen: `SHE WIPES HER TEARS.` → `SHE DOESN'T BEG.` → `POINT BY POINT.`

segments.voice: What was in my power, she says, my heart, was always yours. When I was seized, my body was not in my power. Whose fault is that? And if you meant to give me up, why didn't you tell Hanuman when he found me? Then she asks Lakshmana to build a fire. Lakshmana, angry and pained, builds it at a sign from Rama. Sita walks around Rama in a circle of respect, folds her hands and calls on Agni, the god of fire: if my heart has never turned from Rama, protect me. And she walks into the flames. Why the fire? Because in Hindu tradition Agni is the witness. Offerings poured into a sacred fire pass through him to the gods, and at a Hindu wedding the couple walk around a fire and make their vows with Agni watching. Sita asks the witness of every vow to speak for her. The crowd cries out. Then, Valmiki says, the gods come down, and Brahma tells Rama who he really is: Vishnu himself. Agni rises out of the fire holding Sita, unharmed, her garlands untouched, and declares her pure. Rama answers that he never doubted her, but the world had to see it. Hindus read this scene in many ways. In some later tellings, like the Adhyatma Ramayana and Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, the real Sita was kept safe inside the fire all along, and only a shadow was taken to Lanka. Others hold to Valmiki's version and honor Sita's courage. And many readers today linger longest on her answer. Valmiki gave her those words. They're still there.

660.title: Rama's one wish
660.hook: Rama's father appears, and Rama spends his one wish on forgiveness
660.howItsDone: In North India especially, Diwali remembers Rama's return to Ayodhya, and in many families the days around it are for visits, sweets and calls to relatives, including mending ties.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fire. Sita called on Agni, the witness of every vow, and Agni gave her back. Today, Rama's one wish, and the flight home.

Before they leave Lanka, someone comes that Rama never expected to see again. His father. King Dasharatha, who died of grief after sending his son into exile, appears in the sky in a shining chariot. He holds Rama close for a long time, embraces Lakshmana too, and speaks kindly to Sita. And Rama, with his father in front of him at last, asks for one thing. Not for himself.

Long ago, in his grief, Dasharatha disowned Kaikeyi, who had demanded Rama's exile, and her son Bharata with her. Now Rama asks: take those words back. Be gracious to Kaikeyi and to Bharata. Dasharatha agrees. Think about who Rama is asking for. Kaikeyi's demand cost him fourteen years in the forest, and it broke his father's heart. Rama could ask for anything. He asks for her forgiveness. Hindus call Rama maryada purushottam, the ideal man, the one who lives dharma, right living, all the way through. And old Hindu lists of dharma's marks include kshama, forgiveness, right beside truth and self-control. Here it is in a single wish. Then Indra offers a gift, and again Rama asks for others: bring back the monkeys and bears who died for me, so they can see their families again. Indra grants it, and the fallen rise, whole. Now it's time to go. Rama promised Bharata he'd be back the day the fourteen years ended, and there's no time to walk. So Vibhishana brings out the Pushpaka, the flying chariot that once belonged to Kubera, god of wealth, until Ravana took it. It rises, huge and golden, and Rama points out the places below to Sita: there's where Ravana fell; there's the bridge, still crossing the sea. In many families, Diwali is the season of visits and sweets, and of calling the relative you've drifted from. Rama shows why that call is dharma, not just manners.

661.title: the sandals on the throne
661.hook: Bharata rules fourteen years with Rama's sandals on the throne
661.carry: touching feet is humility that asks a blessing
661.howItsDone: On Diwali and other festival days, many Hindu children touch the feet of their parents and elders and receive a blessing; in many lineages a guru's padukas, sandals, are kept in the shrine and worshiped.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama spent his one wish on forgiveness, and the Pushpaka rose. Your line was forgiveness is part of dharma. Today, the long road home, in reverse.

Over Kishkindha, Sita asks Rama for something. She wants the wives of the monkey leaders, Tara and the others, to come with them to Ayodhya and share the homecoming. So the Pushpaka comes down, and the women climb aboard in their best clothes. Rama agrees at once. The woman who spent months among strangers wants to arrive home surrounded by friends.

Then the flight north becomes the whole story, told backward. Rama points out the places: Rishyamuka, where he met Sugriva; Panchavati, where Ravana took Sita; Chitrakuta, where Bharata came to find him. They land at the sage Bharadvaja's hermitage on the day the fourteen years are complete, and Rama sends Hanuman ahead with a strange instruction: tell Bharata I'm coming, and watch his face. If, after fourteen years, he wants to keep the kingdom, let him have it. Some readers hear a test; others hear respect. Hanuman finds Bharata at Nandigram, outside the capital, living like a hermit in bark clothes. On the throne sit Rama's sandals. Years before, in the forest, Bharata begged Rama to come home, and when Rama wouldn't break his word to their father, Bharata asked for his sandals instead. He set them on the throne and ruled as their servant. Rama is coming, Hanuman tells him, and Bharata falls to the ground with joy. Why sandals? In Hindu tradition, the feet of the one you honor are holy. They're the lowest part of a person, so bowing to them says: I make myself small before you. That's why Hindus bow at the feet of God in the temple, why the padukas of gurus are kept and worshiped in shrines, and why children touch their elders' feet, especially on festival days, and get a blessing back. Bharata held a kingdom for fourteen years and called himself the servant of a pair of sandals.

662.title: the lamps of Diwali
662.hook: Bharata gives back the kingdom, and where Diwali's lamps come from
662.carry: diwali's lamps welcome the light home
662.howItsDone: On Diwali, Hindu families clean the house, light rows of diyas, often do Lakshmi puja in the evening and share sweets; in much of North India the lamps remember Rama's return, and in much of South India the festival remembers Krishna's victory over Narakasura.

segments.voice: Yesterday, paduka: Rama's sandals on Bharata's throne. Your line was touching feet: humility that asks a blessing. Today, the chariot comes down.
screen: `TOUCHING FEET: HUMILITY THAT ASKS A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Why are the lamps lit at Diwali? One answer you'll hear from people who grew up with the festival: because Rama came home, and the whole city lit lamps so he could find his way. It's a lovely picture. So here's a surprise. Open Valmiki's Ramayana to the homecoming and look for the lamps. Valmiki describes flags, flowers, music, roads sprinkled with water, a crowd so big it fills the streets. A city lit by rows of lamps isn't the picture he paints. The lamps seem to have arrived later, as the story moved into the festival. Today, what Valmiki does tell: the homecoming itself, and the man at the center of it, who isn't Rama.
screen: `WHY THE LAMPS?` → `BECAUSE RAMA CAME HOME.` → `WHAT VALMIKI ACTUALLY SAYS.`

segments.voice: Bharata never wanted the throne. When the news comes, his joy fills the chapter. He orders the roads leveled and watered, the city decorated, the musicians out. When the Pushpaka comes into sight, Bharata goes out on foot, carrying the sandals. Rama steps down, Bharata bows, and does what he has waited fourteen years to do: he puts the sandals back on his brother's feet. The kingdom, he says, was a deposit left with me; I'm giving it back. That's Valmiki's homecoming: a promise kept on both sides. So where do the lamps come from? Deepavali means a row of lamps. In much of North India, families light them because Rama came home. Many also welcome Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune, into a clean, bright house that night, and in much of South India the festival remembers Krishna's victory over the demon Narakasura. Different stories, one teaching Hindus hand their children: light wins over darkness, and the good is welcomed home. Neighbors light lamps that season too. Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas, and Jains remember Mahavira's final liberation, each with their own story. Same lamps, their own reasons.

663.hook: Sita's pearls go to Hanuman, the devotee who wants only Rama

663.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep a picture of Hanuman with Rama and Sita in his opened chest, and many Hindus recite the Hanuman Chalisa, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays; many traditional Ramayana recitations end with Rama's coronation, the pattabhishekam.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the lamps of Diwali, and Bharata putting the sandals back on his brother's feet. Today, the crowning, and the last page of the war book.

A coronation is a strange kind of party. Everyone dresses up, there are speeches and gifts, and underneath it the whole room asks one question: what will this person do with the power? Valmiki's crowning of Rama has all the glitter: water from the rivers and the seas, priests chanting, a brother holding the royal umbrella, allies waving the fans. But one moment people treasure is small. It happens after the ceremony, between Sita and Hanuman, over a necklace.
screen: `THE CROWNING.` → `RIVERS AND SEAS, POURED OUT.` → `A NECKLACE.`

segments.voice: First, Rama cuts off the matted hair of the forest years and bathes. Then sacred water is poured over him: the abhisheka, the anointing that makes a king, led by the family priest Vasishtha. Gifts go out to everyone, the monkey and bear allies too. Rama gives Sita a necklace of pearls, and Sita keeps looking from the necklace to Hanuman. Rama sees it. Give it to the one you're most pleased with, he says. She places it around Hanuman's neck: the one who found her in the ashoka grove when no one else could. Valmiki's scene ends there. But Hindus kept telling it. In a much-loved later telling, not in Valmiki, Hanuman bites the pearls open one by one and drops them. The court is shocked. I'm looking for Rama in them, he says, and he isn't there, so what are they worth? Someone mocks him: is Rama in you, then? Hanuman tears open his chest, and there in his heart sit Rama and Sita. You'll find that picture in many Hindu homes. It's bhakti, loving devotion, at its clearest: the devotee wants God, not God's gifts. It's a big reason Hindus pray to Hanuman, the mightiest of Rama's allies, as the model devotee. Then Valmiki closes the war book. Rama rules a long, peaceful age; the rains come on time, and no child dies before a parent. People still call a just order Rama Rajya. Some recitations stop right here. But the Ramayana as it has come down has one more book, and tomorrow it opens.

664.title: Sita sent away
664.hook: gossip reaches the king, and Sita is sent into the forest
664.carry: dharma is subtle, and may be questioned
664.howItsDone: Hindu families and teachers handle the Uttara Kanda in different ways: some recite it in full, many traditional readings stop at the coronation, and many retellings tell Sita's exile with open grief and debate.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the crowning, and Hanuman's pearls. Your line was bhakti keeps god in the heart, and the war book closed on a just reign. Today, the book after the ending.

Many recitations of the Ramayana stop at the crowning, with a pearl necklace and a just reign. But the Ramayana as it has come down has one more book. It's called the Uttara Kanda, the later book, or the book that comes after. It gets six days here, and its argument stays open, the way the tradition has left it. Because this book takes the couple who just came home, and pulls them apart again.
screen: `A CROWNING, AND A JUST REIGN.` → `THEN, ONE MORE BOOK.` → `THE COUPLE, PULLED APART AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Uttara means later; kanda, a section of the poem. The seventh book of Valmiki's Ramayana: many scholars think it was added later; many in the tradition receive it as his own. It comes back to Ayodhya. Rama rules; Sita is pregnant; they walk in the palace gardens. One day Rama asks a companion named Bhadra what the people say about him. Bhadra hesitates, then tells him. They praise the war. But some say: how can the king take back a wife who lived in Ravana's house? If the king allows it, we'll have to put up with it from our own wives. Rama calls his brothers. He has decided: Sita will be taken to the forest near the sage Valmiki's hermitage, and left there. He forbids them to argue. Once again it falls to Lakshmana, with the charioteer Sumantra. Sita thinks she's going to visit the hermits, as she had asked. At the Ganga, Lakshmana breaks down and tells her the truth. The poem shows Rama in grief and Sita blameless, both at once. This is the hardest scene in the Ramayana, and Hindus have argued with it for centuries. The Mahabharata says more than once that dharma is subtle: a king's duty to his people and a husband's duty to his wife can pull apart. Some defend Rama's choice as a king's sacrifice. The playwright Bhavabhuti built a whole drama on his grief. Women's songs in many Indian languages take Sita's side. Many teachers say wrestling with this scene isn't disrespect; it's part of the tradition.
screen: `UTTARA KANDA: THE LATER BOOK.` · `WHAT ARE THE PEOPLE SAYING?` · `SITA LEFT AT THE GANGA.` · `RAMA GRIEVES. SITA IS BLAMELESS.` · then, large: `DHARMA IS SUBTLE.`

segments.voice: There's an old Hindu word for this kind of practice: manana, turning a teaching over in your mind after you've heard it. Picture Rama, alone, deciding. Then Sita, on the far bank. Don't settle who was right. Notice where your sympathy goes, and let it stay with both. If you'd like to pray, ask for clear seeing; if not, just breathe and hold the question.

665.title: Lava and Kusha
665.hook: Valmiki takes Sita in, and teaches her twin sons to sing the Ramayana
665.carry: the ramayana lives by being sung
665.tomorrow: Sita goes home to the earth
665.howItsDone: Lava and Kusha are familiar in temple paintings, folk plays and children's books; and Hindus still learn the Ramayana by ear, in temple kathas, Ramlila plays at Dussehra and songs at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Uttara Kanda opened. Gossip reached the king, and Lakshmana left Sita by the Ganga. Your line was dharma is subtle, and may be questioned. Today, two boys are born in a hermitage.

Sita doesn't stay alone on the riverbank for long. Young hermits find her weeping and run to tell their teacher, and he comes down to the water himself. It's Valmiki, the poet, the man who, at the very start of this serial, heard a bird's cry and found the first verse. He takes Sita by the hand and walks her to the women of the hermitage. The poet of the story has just stepped into it.
screen: `THE HERMITS FIND HER.` → `VALMIKI COMES DOWN TO THE WATER.` → `THE POET STEPS INTO THE STORY.`

segments.voice: Valmiki tells Sita he knows she's done nothing wrong, and gives her a home among the hermit women. Months later, she gives birth to twins. Valmiki prepares protective rites for the newborns with kusha grass, the sacred grass of Vedic ritual. The elder is touched with the tops of the grass, so he is Kusha; the younger with the lower part, the lava, so he is Lava. Then Valmiki folds the whole poem back on itself. As the boys grow, he teaches them the Ramayana: this very song, with their father as its hero. They learn it by heart and sing it beautifully. Years later, Rama holds a great horse sacrifice, the ashvamedha. Valmiki brings the boys, and they sing the poem in the open, day after day. Crowds gather. Rama hears it, is moved, and doesn't yet know whose sons are singing. The poem's very first book opens with Kusha and Lava singing it before Rama, so the frame was this moment all along. Here's the teaching. The Ramayana was made to be sung and heard, and Hindus still keep it that way: a grandmother singing over the stove, a Ram katha at the temple that runs for days, the Ramlila plays at Dussehra, a family reading a chapter aloud together. Hearing sacred stories, shravana, is counted as a form of devotion in itself. And the first people to carry this one were two children who learned it by heart.
screen: `VALMIKI TAKES SITA IN.` · `KUSHA AND LAVA: NAMED FOR GRASS.` · `THE SONS LEARN THEIR FATHER'S STORY.` · `SHRAVANA: HEARING IS DEVOTION.` · then, large: `A STORY MADE TO BE SUNG.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus sing a simple line for Rama: Sri Ram, Jai Ram, Jai Jai Ram. Say it or sing it softly, slowly, for two minutes, and listen to your own voice the way the crowd listened to the twins. If you don't pray, hum a song someone in your family taught you, and notice who you learned it from.
